paragraphs: Learning to rank online means improving an ordered list of documents from users’ interactions with it. The difficulty is that clicks depend on how people inspect the list, not just on document quality. Algorithms designed around one particular model of clicking may lose their convergence guarantees when users behave according to another model.

The paper introduces BatchRank, an algorithm designed for a broader class of click models. That class includes both the cascade and position-based models, two fundamental ways of describing interactions with ranked results. Its contribution is therefore a shared learning approach across multiple models, rather than a separate algorithm tailored to each one.

The authors establish a gap-dependent upper bound on cumulative regret, measuring the cost of learning over successive rounds. In evaluations on web search queries, BatchRank outperforms ranked bandits and proves more robust than CascadeKL-UCB. These findings support the practical value of broader model coverage, while the theoretical guarantee remains tied to the specified class of click models.
icml-2017-online-learning-to-rank-in-sto.tldr: BatchRank learns document rankings with regret guarantees across a broad class of click models and shows improved robustness in web search evaluations.

paragraphs: A recurrent network processes a sequence by repeatedly updating its internal state. Some tasks require a complicated transformation between consecutive steps, but making that transformation deeper can make training difficult. The paper addresses this problem even in the setting of Long Short-Term Memory networks, which already provide a specialized recurrent architecture.

The authors first analyze recurrent networks using Gersgorin’s circle theorem. This mathematical perspective clarifies issues in modeling and optimization and gives additional insight into the LSTM cell. Motivated by that analysis, they introduce Recurrent Highway Networks, extending the LSTM architecture so that each step-to-step transition can contain more than one layer of computation.

Language modeling experiments show substantial benefits from this added transition depth. On Penn Treebank, increasing depth from one to ten reduces word-level perplexity from 90.6 to 65.4 without increasing the parameter count. On text8 and enwik8 character prediction, the models surpass previous reported results and reach 1.27 bits per character. The results show that deeper transitions can improve predictive performance without simply enlarging the parameter budget.
icml-2017-recurrent-highway-networks-750.tldr: Recurrent Highway Networks deepen the computation between sequence steps, improving language modeling without requiring more parameters.

paragraphs: Binary classification assigns one of two outcomes to each example. Adding a quantitative fairness requirement changes the learning problem: the classifier must control prediction error while satisfying constraints on its behavior. This paper develops a systematic way to handle that constrained problem, focusing on two established fairness definitions while also covering many others.

The central idea is to translate fair classification into a sequence of cost-sensitive classification tasks. In these tasks, different prediction mistakes carry different costs. The solutions are used to produce a randomized classifier with the lowest empirical error subject to the desired fairness constraints. The error claim concerns performance on the observed data, and the fairness target is the chosen mathematical definition.

The authors introduce two such reductions, both compatible with any representation of the underlying cost-sensitive classifier. This flexibility makes the approach applicable across classifier designs. Experiments on several datasets compare favorably with earlier baselines, supporting the usefulness of expressing fairness requirements through a reusable classification interface.
icml-2018-a-reductions-approach-to-fair-.tldr: The paper reduces fairness-constrained binary classification to cost-sensitive learning tasks that yield an empirically optimal randomized classifier.

paragraphs: Rank aggregation combines comparisons into an overall ranking, whether those comparisons involve two alternatives or larger groups. Spectral methods approach this problem through random walks. The paper introduces accelerated spectral ranking, or ASR, to make this computation faster while retaining consistent estimation under the Bradley-Terry-Luce and multinomial logit comparison models.

The acceleration comes from constructing a random walk with a faster mixing time than those used by earlier algorithms. In plain terms, the walk approaches its stable behavior more quickly. The authors also improve bounds on the number of observations needed to recover model parameters, including general bounds for multiway comparisons under any connected comparison graph.

A message-passing interpretation suggests that ASR could be implemented in a decentralized, distributed fashion. Experiments on real and synthetic datasets show speed improvements of orders of magnitude over existing algorithms. Together, the results address both computational effort and data requirements, with consistency and parameter-recovery claims grounded in the stated comparison models and connectivity condition.
icml-2018-accelerated-spectral-ranking-e.tldr: ASR accelerates spectral ranking through faster-mixing random walks while improving parameter-recovery bounds under standard comparison models.

paragraphs: Learning between domains from unpaired data means using examples from both domains without requiring a matched counterpart for every observation. This can reduce the need for paired training data in structured prediction tasks such as image segmentation. The paper examines a restriction in CycleGAN that limits which relationships between domains it can represent effectively.

CycleGAN assumes that the mapping is approximately deterministic and one-to-one. That assumption is poorly suited to tasks where an example can have multiple valid counterparts and the relationship works that way in both directions. The authors propose Augmented CycleGAN to learn these many-to-many mappings, making the intended relationship between domains more flexible.

The paper evaluates the model both qualitatively and quantitatively on several image datasets. These evaluations examine its behavior in the setting that motivates the new model. The central contribution is expanding the type of mapping that can be learned from unpaired data, addressing ambiguity between domains without requiring that each input correspond to one predetermined output.
icml-2018-augmented-cyclegan-learning-ma.tldr: Augmented CycleGAN learns flexible many-to-many relationships between domains from unpaired data.

paragraphs: AutoPrognosis automates the design of prediction pipelines for clinical prognosis. Rather than requiring researchers to manually choose a complete modeling configuration, it searches for effective ensembles of pipelines. The challenge is that these configurations occupy a large hyperparameter space, making efficient search an important part of the system.

Its batched Bayesian optimization procedure learns a lower-dimensional decomposition of that space while searching it. Pipeline performance is modeled with a Gaussian process, and a sparse additive kernel with a Dirichlet prior represents similarities between baseline algorithms. These components let the search learn structure in the choices it is evaluating, rather than treating every configuration as unrelated.

The system also uses information from similar patient cohorts to initialize the search by adjusting its priors. For clinicians, it presents logical association rules connecting patient features to predicted risk groups. Evaluation across ten cardiovascular patient cohorts demonstrates the system’s utility, bringing together automated pipeline selection, experience from other cohorts, and explanations of predicted risk within one prognostic modeling workflow.
icml-2018-autoprognosis-automated-clinic.tldr: AutoPrognosis combines structured Bayesian optimization, cohort-based prior knowledge, and rule explanations to automate clinical prognostic modeling.

paragraphs: Probabilistic graphical models need a normalizing constant, called the partition function, to turn their assigned weights into probabilities. Computing it exactly is generally intractable. Approximation is therefore essential, but even successful iterative variational methods can give poor answers or fail to converge on difficult problems.

This paper takes a different computational route: summing over variables in sequence. The authors combine ideas from mini-bucket elimination with tensor networks and renormalization group methods from statistical physics. The resulting algorithms approximate the partition function through this sequential calculation, avoiding the need for an iterative variational procedure to settle at a solution.

The authors describe the methods as convergence-free and report good empirical performance on synthetic and real-world benchmark models, including difficult instances. That finding matters because convergence failures are one of the motivating weaknesses of existing approaches. The contribution is a robust alternative for approximate normalization; being convergence-free describes how the computation proceeds, while the reported quality of its approximations is supported by the experiments.
icml-2018-bucket-renormalization-for-app.tldr: Bucket renormalization approximates partition functions through sequential summation, with strong empirical performance without iterative convergence.

paragraphs: Identity and equivalence testing ask whether sampled data agree with a specified distribution or whether two sampled distributions agree with one another. This paper studies these questions for discrete populations while requiring differential privacy for individuals. The aim is to make reliable statistical decisions without needing an excessive number of observations to provide privacy.

The authors develop sample-efficient private testers for both problems. Their theoretical results substantially improve earlier algorithms for identity testing and provide the first results for private equivalence testing. The conceptual finding is that private hypothesis testing can come close to the sample efficiency of testing without privacy, so privacy need not always impose a large data burden.

Experiments on synthetic data illustrate small type I and type II errors, covering both kinds of mistaken testing decisions. These results occur with sample sizes smaller than the size of the distributions’ domains. The experiments support the theoretical message by showing useful testing behavior without requiring observations proportional to the entire domain.
icml-2018-differentially-private-identit.tldr: The paper develops private distribution testers that can approach non-private sample efficiency and perform well on synthetic data.

paragraphs: Making a learned representation understandable often involves training for both accuracy and interpretability at once. That can reduce accuracy and cannot directly help a model that has already been trained. This paper offers two frameworks that use limited side information to define which aspects of a representation should be interpretable.

The first provides a new view of an existing generative or discriminative model’s representation. A generative model and a flexible, invertible transformation produce an interpretable representation without losing accuracy. An active learning extension chooses useful side information to request, allowing a person to guide the meaning of interpretability rather than leaving it entirely predetermined.

The second framework jointly learns a representation that retains as much information as possible about the side information while compressing factors deemed non-interpretable. This connects interpretability with compression and regularization. The authors also introduce an evaluation metric and report state-of-the-art results across three datasets using their two algorithms, supporting both adapting existing representations and learning new ones.
icml-2018-discovering-interpretable-repr.tldr: Two frameworks use limited side information to make existing or newly learned representations interpretable.

paragraphs: Latent-variable models learn hidden representations while modeling observed data. Because maximizing the data likelihood is often intractable, training commonly maximizes an evidence lower bound, or ELBO. This paper shows theoretically and empirically that optimizing likelihood, exactly or approximately, does not necessarily produce a useful latent representation.

The authors derive lower and upper variational bounds on the mutual information between inputs and latent variables. These bounds support a rate-distortion view of learning: how much information the representation retains is considered alongside how accurately the model reconstructs the input. This separates properties that a single ELBO value can conceal.

Using that framework, the paper identifies a family of models with identical ELBO values but different quantitative and qualitative behavior. Equal training-objective scores therefore need not mean equivalent representations. The framework also suggests a simple method to ensure that models with powerful stochastic decoders use their latent code, addressing the possibility that a capable decoder otherwise ignores the representation it was intended to exploit.
icml-2018-fixing-a-broken-elbo-02d643b1e.tldr: The paper shows why equal ELBO scores can hide different representation quality and develops an information-based framework to address this.

paragraphs: The paper studies Thompson sampling for infinite-horizon linear quadratic control, where states and actions are continuous, dynamics are linear, and costs are quadratic. Its focus is frequentist regret: the accumulated cost of learning in a fixed but unknown environment. This differs from analyzing average performance over a prior distribution of environments.

For one-dimensional systems, the authors prove a regret bound of order square root of T. This improves the previous T to the two-thirds bound and matches rates established for an optimistic approach and a Bayesian analysis. The improvement gives a stronger guarantee on how quickly the cost of uncertainty becomes small relative to the duration of control.

A key ingredient is a new bound on regret caused by switching policies. That bound applies to linear quadratic systems of any dimension and permits parameter and policy updates at every step. The full square-root regret result is proved for one dimension; simulations support, but do not establish, the conjecture that it extends to multiple dimensions.
icml-2018-improved-regret-bounds-for-tho.tldr: Thompson sampling achieves square-root frequentist regret in one-dimensional linear quadratic control through a sharper analysis of policy switching.

paragraphs: Empirical risk minimization chooses a model by minimizing its loss on observed data. This paper analyzes that procedure through mutual information, connecting information-theoretic quantities with established measures of learnability. It treats both classification with zero-one loss and learning problems whose losses are strongly convex.

Under the Axiom of Choice, the authors prove that an ERM rule with vanishing mutual information exists exactly when the loss class has finite VC dimension. For strongly convex losses, they establish an asymptotic information bound in terms of the number of model parameters, using a central limit theorem developed in the paper. They also apply the analysis to excess risk in stochastic convex optimization.

The theory leads to two applications. A simple parallelization scheme can scale strongly convex ERM to large datasets with provable guarantees. A new information criterion also provides a way to select models. Experiments show that this criterion outperforms AIC and BIC in the reported evaluations, connecting the theoretical analysis to practical choices about computation and model complexity.
icml-2018-information-theoretic-guarante.tldr: Information bounds for empirical risk minimization connect learnability with mutual information and support parallel optimization and model selection.

paragraphs: A sample from a discrete distribution may reveal only part of its underlying structure. INSPECTRE studies how to estimate properties of that distribution while protecting the individuals represented in the sample. The objective combines a specified estimation accuracy with a specified level of differential privacy.

The paper considers support size, support coverage, and entropy. These describe different aspects of a distribution, including how many possible outcomes it has and how its probability is spread. The authors build on existing estimators that work with sublinear sample complexity, analyzing how sensitive their outputs are to changes in the sample so that privacy can be incorporated.

For several of these properties, the authors prove nearly tight bounds on the sample size required to satisfy accuracy and privacy together. Theory and experiments show that the extra cost of privacy is negligible in a variety of settings. The qualified conclusion is that protecting samples can be compatible with efficient estimation of distributional structure, even when the observations do not exhaust the possible outcomes.
icml-2018-inspectre-privately-estimating.tldr: INSPECTRE estimates discrete distribution properties privately, with nearly tight sample bounds and negligible privacy costs in several settings.

paragraphs: The optimization setting in this paper has an important distinction: the overall objective is convex, even though the individual functions being averaged can be nonconvex. This structure appears in computational machinery for PCA, SVD, regularized Newton methods, and accelerated nonconvex optimization. The goal is to exploit the finite-sum structure efficiently despite the behavior of its individual terms.

Katyusha X modifies the established SVRG method by adding a single line corresponding to momentum. The authors prove that this change produces an accelerated stochastic algorithm for the stated problem class. The contribution is both an acceleration result and a direct way to apply momentum when the component functions are nonconvex but their average is convex.

The method also has a linear parallel speed-up result when using mini-batches. This connects its optimization improvement with the ability to process grouped computations in parallel. The guarantees concern the specified sum-of-nonconvex setting, so the convexity of the aggregate objective remains central to understanding what the paper establishes.
icml-2018-katyusha-x-simple-momentum-met.tldr: Katyusha X adds a momentum step to SVRG, provably accelerating convex objectives composed of nonconvex terms.

paragraphs: The paper studies three-dimensional shapes represented as point clouds. It introduces a deep autoencoder that compresses these shapes into learned representations and reconstructs them with state-of-the-art quality and generalization. Those representations also outperform existing methods on 3D recognition tasks, making them useful beyond reconstruction alone.

Simple algebraic operations in the learned representation enable semantic part editing, shape analogies, and interpolation. The representation also supports shape completion. The authors then compare several ways to generate point clouds: GANs trained directly on the points, GANs trained in the autoencoder’s fixed latent space, and Gaussian mixture models trained in that space.

To assess generation, they introduce measures of sample fidelity and diversity based on matching sets of point clouds. Latent-space GANs improve substantially over the raw-point approach, but Gaussian mixture models give the best overall results across the reported generalization, fidelity, and diversity evaluation. This finding emphasizes the value of the learned representation: a comparatively simple generator can work especially well when it operates in that space.
icml-2018-learning-representations-and-g.tldr: A point-cloud autoencoder supports recognition, shape editing, and generation, with latent-space Gaussian mixtures performing best overall in the evaluation.

paragraphs: Estimating heterogeneous treatment effects means learning how a treatment’s effect varies across cases. Observational data make this difficult because the counterfactual outcome is unavailable: the data do not reveal both outcomes for the same case. The paper develops guidance for estimator design by characterizing fundamental estimation limits and conditions under which they can be reached.

The analysis finds that the relative importance of modeling choices changes with sample size. Within the setting analyzed, selection bias matters in small-sample regimes, while modeling treated and control outcomes becomes the performance bottleneck with large samples. This identifies a changing allocation of modeling effort rather than a single concern that dominates every data regime.

Guided by the theory, the authors construct an estimator using non-stationary Gaussian processes with doubly robust hyperparameters. In a standard semi-synthetic simulation, it outperforms the state of the art, and existing algorithms behave in ways consistent with the analysis. The contribution joins theoretical limits with a practical estimator designed around the sources of difficulty those limits reveal.
icml-2018-limits-of-estimating-heterogen.tldr: The paper characterizes treatment-effect estimation limits across sample sizes and uses them to design a successful Gaussian-process estimator.

paragraphs: Different measurement technologies can describe the same biological system in different spaces. Integrating those measurements requires aligning their manifolds, the structures formed by the observations, so that corresponding biological information can be brought together. The paper argues that recent GAN-based correspondence methods do not explicitly achieve the required manifold alignment.

MAGAN, the Manifold Aligning GAN, is designed to align two manifolds so that related points in their respective measurement spaces line up. This makes the relationship between observations central to the integration task. The intended result is a combined view of the underlying system that respects which observations are related across measurement types.

The authors demonstrate the approach in single-cell biology using genomic measurements from single-cell RNA sequencing and proteomic measurements from mass cytometry on cells from the same tissue. MAGAN improves known correlations between measured markers compared with other recently proposed models. Those correlations provide evidence that the learned alignment preserves meaningful biological relationships across the two forms of measurement.
icml-2018-magan-aligning-biological-mani.tldr: MAGAN aligns biological measurement spaces so related points correspond, improving known marker correlations in single-cell data integration.

paragraphs: Regret measures how much an online learner loses compared with the best fixed strategy chosen after seeing the entire sequence. Standard bounds often grow with the square root of the number of rounds. A first-order bound instead scales with the square root of the best strategy’s cumulative loss, which can be much smaller.

Such guarantees were already available through modest changes to standard algorithms in full-information and multi-armed bandit settings. Obtaining them for contextual bandits remained an open problem because existing techniques appeared insufficient. The paper addresses this gap with a new strategy that augments the policy space available to the learner.

The result resolves the stated open problem by establishing a first-order regret bound for contextual bandits. Its significance is that the guarantee can reflect how well the comparison strategy actually performs, rather than relying only on how long learning continues. When that strategy incurs little loss, this gives a more informative performance guarantee than a bound governed by the time horizon.
icml-2018-make-the-minority-great-again-.tldr: Augmenting the policy space yields a contextual-bandit regret bound that scales with the best strategy’s loss rather than the time horizon.

paragraphs: Meta-learning uses experience from previous tasks to make new tasks easier to learn. This paper assumes that future tasks are related to earlier ones, creating an opportunity to capture shared structure. At the same time, the learner needs enough flexibility to adapt when a new task has unfamiliar aspects.

The authors extend PAC-Bayes generalization bounds to this setting. Experience is represented through a distribution over hypotheses learned from observed tasks, which supplies an experience-dependent prior for future learning. This gives a mathematical framework for deciding how prior knowledge can inform a new task while still allowing adaptation to its data.

From the bounds, the authors derive an objective and a gradient-based learning algorithm, which they implement for deep neural networks. Numerical experiments demonstrate effectiveness and improved performance through meta-learning. They also show how prior information appears at different network levels. The work therefore connects a theory of generalization across related tasks with a trainable mechanism for transferring experience through priors.
icml-2018-meta-learning-by-adjusting-pri.tldr: Extended PAC-Bayes bounds guide learning experience-dependent priors that help neural networks adapt to related new tasks.

paragraphs: Learning a Bayesian network becomes especially uncertain when there are more observed variables than data points. A Bayesian approach can represent that uncertainty and incorporate prior structural knowledge, but the number of possible directed acyclic graphs makes inference difficult. Existing order-based sampling methods also restrict useful priors and can have exponential dependence on maximum indegree.

The proposed method uses empirical conditional independence tests to focus on a high-probability graph associated with each ordering of the variables. This creates an alternative approximation to the posterior over network structures. The idea reduces the structural possibilities considered through information extracted from the data while retaining a Bayesian treatment of uncertainty.

The authors show that the approach permits flexible structural priors, removes runtime dependence on maximum indegree, and provides provably good posterior approximations. On several datasets it also improves accuracy, scalability, and sampler mixing. These results address both the statistical need to represent plausible networks and the computational difficulty of exploring a large space of possible structures.
icml-2018-minimal-i-map-mcmc-for-scalabl.tldr: Conditional independence tests guide a scalable approximation to Bayesian network posteriors while allowing flexible structural priors.

paragraphs: Feature selection becomes difficult when datasets have billions of dimensions, because even storing a full feature vector can be infeasible. Feature hashing helps make computation manageable, but loses the interpretability of individual features. This paper addresses the need to select useful, identifiable features under severe memory constraints.

MISSION combines stochastic gradient descent with a Count-Sketch data structure that maintains an efficient representation of features in memory. The framework retains the simplicity associated with hashing while preserving feature interpretability. Its stated working-memory requirement is O(log²(p)), where p is the number of dimensions, allowing memory to grow slowly as dimensionality increases.

Experiments demonstrate accurate and efficient feature selection on real-world datasets with billions of dimensions. The result matters because the memory representation is part of what makes selection possible at this scale, rather than merely speeding up an already feasible full-vector method. The framework links large-scale learning with the ability to retain meaningful feature identities for understanding the selected inputs.
icml-2018-mission-ultra-large-scale-feat.tldr: MISSION uses Count-Sketches during stochastic gradient descent to select interpretable features from billion-dimensional data with very small working memory.

paragraphs: Many datasets contain naturally grouped observed variables, and understanding interactions among those groups can be as important as generating realistic samples. Traditional latent factor models offer an interpretable approach but assume linear correlation structure. This paper develops an output-interpretable variational autoencoder, oi-VAE, for modeling more complex relationships in grouped data.

The model combines generators specific to each output group with a prior that encourages sparsity. This structure connects the hidden representation to identifiable groups of observations while allowing nonlinear relationships between latent and observed variables. The design makes the organization of the outputs part of how the generative model is built.

Experiments with motion capture and MEG data demonstrate meaningful interpretations of the learned model. In those settings, the authors also find that the regularization built into oi-VAE can improve generalization and the learned generative process. The result shows that interpretability-oriented structure can bring predictive modeling benefits as well as making relationships among groups easier to understand.
icml-2018-oi-vae-output-interpretable-va.tldr: oi-VAE combines group-specific generators and sparsity to learn interpretable nonlinear factors, with generalization benefits in the studied datasets.

paragraphs: In lifelong reinforcement learning, an agent encounters a sequence of tasks drawn from a task distribution. Previous experience can provide a useful starting point, but choosing what to transfer is itself a learning problem. This paper studies two forms of initialization: the policy the agent starts with and the values it assigns before learning a new task.

For policy transfer, the authors identify initial policies that optimize expected performance over the task distribution. They consider increasingly complex classes of policies and task distributions, then compare the best policies from these classes empirically on simple task distributions. This makes the starting policy a deliberate choice based on expected performance across tasks.

For value transfer, they investigate initializations that preserve PAC learning guarantees while minimizing the learning required by two algorithms. This produces MaxQInit, a practical method for transferring value-function information. Experiments show good performance in simple lifelong reinforcement learning settings, demonstrating how prior experience can initialize learning while retaining the guarantees considered in the analysis.
icml-2018-policy-and-value-transfer-in-l.tldr: The paper studies effective initial policies and introduces MaxQInit for value transfer that preserves PAC guarantees in lifelong reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Bipartite matching allocates items on one side of a graph to eligible recipients on the other. The paper studies a simple distributed procedure that assigns each recipient a priority score, initially equal for everyone. Items are allocated in proportion to those scores, providing a direct rule for sharing available opportunities.

After each round, scores decrease for recipients receiving too much allocation and increase for those receiving too little. The authors prove that this process reaches a fractional b-matching within a factor of 1 minus epsilon of optimal in O(log(n)/epsilon²) rounds. They also extend the proportional allocation approach and its convergence results to maximum weighted matching.

The algorithm can additionally be tuned to produce maximum matchings with high entropy. In this setting, high entropy implies certain diversity and fairness properties, including anonymity, that are useful in advertising and machine learning applications. The contribution combines a lightweight allocation mechanism with approximation guarantees and a way to favor a more diverse distribution of assignments.
icml-2018-proportional-allocation-simple.tldr: Iterative proportional allocation efficiently approximates fractional matching and can produce high-entropy matchings with specified diversity and fairness properties.

paragraphs: State abstraction compresses the representation an agent uses to learn and act. In lifelong reinforcement learning, such compression could reduce computational and data demands across multiple tasks. The challenge is to retain distinctions that matter for good decisions while simplifying enough to help exploration, credit assignment, and generalization.

The paper introduces two classes of abstractions. Transitive state abstractions have an optimal form that can be computed efficiently. PAC state abstractions provide guarantees with respect to a distribution of tasks. Combining these ideas yields transitive PAC abstractions, which the authors show can be acquired efficiently while preserving near-optimal behavior.

Experiments in simple domains show reduced sample complexity, meaning that the compressed representation can reduce the experience required for learning. The paper also identifies pathological cases in which state abstraction harms performance. Together, these results explain both the promise and the risk of compression: the proposed family has useful guarantees, but abstraction in general does not automatically preserve what an agent needs across tasks.
icml-2018-state-abstractions-for-lifelon.tldr: Transitive PAC state abstractions can be learned efficiently and preserve near-optimal behavior across tasks, though abstraction can also harm performance.
